voltage-drop-calculator.name: Voltage Drop Calculator
voltage-drop-calculator.tagline: Check voltage drop over wire runs — single or three phase, copper or aluminum.
voltage-drop-calculator.metaTitle: Voltage Drop Calculator – Wire Size & Drop % | JaurTools
voltage-drop-calculator.metaDescription: Free voltage drop calculator. Enter voltage, phase, wire size, length and current for copper or aluminum — get drop volts, % and max current, 100% in your browser.
voltage-drop-calculator.keywords: voltage drop calculator, wire voltage drop, cable size voltage drop, voltage drop formula, single phase voltage drop
voltage-drop-calculator.quickAnswer: Voltage drop grows with current and cable length, and shrinks with thicker wire: single-phase drop is 2×ρ×L×I/A. A 30 m run of 2.5 mm² copper at 16 A on 230 V drops 6.60 V (2.87%) — fine for power circuits (limit 5%) but over the 3% lighting limit. Upsize the wire or shorten the run to fix it.
keyFacts: Voltage drop is the volts lost heating the cable itself — the load receives supply minus drop.
Copper resistivity is 0.0172 Ω·mm²/m; aluminum is 0.0282 — aluminum drops about 64% more for the same size.
Single-phase uses 2× (out and back); three-phase uses √3× for line-to-line drop.
Common limits: 3% for lighting, 5% for power circuits (per IEC guidance).
Doubling the wire cross-section halves the drop; doubling the length doubles it.
Undersized cable runs hot: drop is wasted energy and a fire risk at high currents.
howTo: Enter the supply voltage (e.g. 230 V single phase, 400 V three phase).
Choose single or three phase, and copper or aluminum conductor.
Enter the wire cross-section in mm², the one-way cable length in meters, and the load current in amps.
Read the voltage drop in volts and percent, the voltage at the load, and the max current for a 5% drop.
If the verdict is over the limit, increase the wire size until it passes.
voltage-drop-calculator.formula:
Single phase: Vd = 2 × ρ × L × I ÷ A
Three phase:  Vd = √3 × ρ × L × I ÷ A
ρ copper = 0.0172, ρ aluminum = 0.0282 Ω·mm²/m
Drop % = Vd ÷ V × 100
voltage-drop-calculator.workedExample:
230 V, single phase, copper, 2.5 mm², 30 m, 16 A.
Vd = 2 × 0.0172 × 30 × 16 ÷ 2.5 = 16.512 ÷ 2.5 = 6.60 V
Drop % = 6.60 ÷ 230 × 100 = 2.87%
Voltage at load = 230 − 6.60 = 223.4 V
Max current for 5% = 0.05 × 230 × 2.5 ÷ (2 × 0.0172 × 30) = 27.9 A
Verdict: 2.87% is within the 5% power limit (but above the 3% lighting limit).
benefits: Catches undersized cable before installation — the cheapest time to fix it.
Covers single and three phase plus both conductor materials in one tool.
Max-current readout tells you the safe headroom at a glance.
Honest physics with no hidden fudge factors.
limitations: A steady-state resistive calculation: it ignores reactance, which matters for large cables and long three-phase runs.
Assumes conductor at ~20 °C: hot cables have higher resistance and slightly more drop.
Does not check thermal current rating (ampacity) — a wire can pass the drop test yet still overheat; check both.
Not a substitute for a licensed electrician: wiring must follow your local electrical code.

faqs.a: The voltage lost along the cable due to its resistance. The load sees the supply voltage minus the drop — too much drop makes motors run hot and lights dim.

faqs.q: What is an acceptable voltage drop?
faqs.a: IEC guidance commonly used: 3% for lighting circuits, 5% for other power circuits, measured from the supply origin to the load.
In a balanced three-phase system the line-to-line drop relates to phase current through √3 by the geometry of the three phasors 120° apart.
Aluminum's resistivity is about 64% higher than copper's, so the same size drops more. Equivalent performance needs roughly two standard sizes larger aluminum.
Yes — copper resistance rises about 0.4% per °C. A cable running hot at 70 °C drops roughly 20% more than this 20 °C calculation shows.

faqs.q: Length means one-way or round trip?
faqs.a: Enter the one-way cable length. The formula already accounts for the return path (the factor of 2 in single phase).

labels.lengthHint: The formula accounts for the return path itself.
labels.currentHint: Steady current drawn by the load.
labels.okLabel: Within 3% — fine for lighting and power.
labels.warnLabel: 3–5% — OK for power circuits, too high for lighting.
